rv.q: These plays are not going to do anything much in the way of reputation burnishing for their three celebrated authors — and certainly none is required — but they are packed with nifty zingers and have been directed by John Turturro with a boisterous flair for socking home the borscht-belt humor.

Home of the San Francisco Chronicle By MARK KENNEDY, AP In this theater image released by Boneau Bryan Brown, Danny Hoch, left, and Jason Kravits perform in "Talking Cure" one of three one-act comedies comprising "Relatively Speaking" in New York.
But Talking Cure is the least satisfying item on a stale menu.
Unfortunately, throwbacks, if they are to get somewhere, need to have aim, momentum and a sense of direction.
Although Allen has dragged the corny borscht-belt routines out of the trunk in affectionate homage, bad jokes are still bad jokes.
You may also wonder why theatergoers aren't rioting for a refund.
The theory is impeccable, the results disastrous.
As something charging Broadway prices, it’s relatively disgusting.
While its premise may particularly appeal to men of a certain age who fancy women half their age, the laughter was co-ed.
However, the preceding two pieces provide mixed results.

But given the estimable writers of the pieces, Ethan Coen, Elaine May and Woody Allen, and the proven talents of the high-profile ensemble, it’s difficult to not be disappointed by the production, which should be the comic pinnacle for the Broadway season.
Relatively Speaking is, comparatively speaking, far from any of its creators' finest work.
For these accounts of homegrown neuroses — by veteran wits Elaine May, Ethan Coen and Woody Allen— offer both disarming highs and disappointing lows.
Unfortunately, “George is Dead,” the second one-act of the evening takes a thin and obvious premise, exacerbating the character’s motives until it becomes anxiety provoking to sit through.
This is just an old-fashioned, third-rate farce and is hardly worthy of being done on Broadway.
Relatively speaking, Relatively Speaking is a bust.
Credit both Thomas and Lisa Emery for giving it their best shot but what really dies here is the comedy.
That this level of writing talent could produce such a lethargic, laugh-free evening is a mystery and a tremendous disappointment.
It’s all very loud, very fast and remarkably pointless.

cn.t: Mixed reviews for this trio of one-acts by Allen, Coen, and May, with critics finding sporadic laughs but mostly disappointment given the legendary writers' pedigree. Allen's closer earns the most praise.
